{{Notability|date=March 2026}}

In [[graph theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], an '''equitable partition''' of the vertex set ''V'' of a graph ''G'' = (''V, E'') is a [[Partition of a set|partition]] of ''V'' such that, for any pair of vertices ''u'' and ''v'' in the same set of the partition and any set ''B'' of the partition, both ''u'' and ''v'' have the same number of neighbors in ''B''.

More precisely, one represents <math>V = V_1 \cup V_2 \cup \cdots \cup V_r</math> where every vertex is contained in exactly one "cell" <math>V_i</math>, the edges within each cell form a [[regular graph]], and for any two distinct cells <math>V_i</math> and <math>V_j</math> and every vertex <math>v_i \in V_i</math>, the number of edges <math>v_iv_j</math> such that <math>v_j \in V_j</math> is a constant <math>b_{ij}</math>, independent of the choice of <math>v_i \in V_i</math>.

The ''characteristic matrix'' <math>P</math> of the partition has a row for each vertex and a column for each cell, with 1 in row <math>v</math> and column <math>V_i</math> if <math>v \in V_i</math>, otherwise 0.

Equitable partitions are important for simplifying calculations involving [[Adjacency matrix|adjacency]] and related matrices of large graphs.

==Equitable partitions from automorphisms==

The orbits of a group of [[Graph automorphism|automorphism]]s of ''G'' form an equitable partition of ''V''.<ref>Godsil and Royle (2001), Section 9.3.</ref>  This fact can assist in studying eigenvalues of graphs with [[Vertex-transitive graph|vertex-transitive]] automorphism group.  It can also assist in determining [[Graph isomorphism problem|isomorphism of graphs]].<ref>McKay (1981).</ref>

==Matrix use==

Equitable partitions allow collapsing <math>|V| \times |V|</math> graphical matrices into smaller, <math>r \times r</math> matrices while preserving the set of [[Eigenvalues#Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices|eigenvalues]].  Thus, they can facilitate [[spectral graph theory]].<ref>Godsil and Royle (2001), Section 9.3.</ref>  For example, if <math>\pi</math> is an equitable partition of <math>G</math>, then the characteristic polynomial of <math>A(G)</math> is divisible by that of <math>A(G/\pi)</math>, where <math>G/\pi</math> is a weighted [[directed graph]] formed by collapsing each cell to a single vertex.<ref>Godsil and Royle (2001), Theorem 9.3.3.</ref> Thus, the eigenvalues of <math>A(G/\pi)</math> are also eigenvalues of <math>A(G)</math>, but <math>A(G/\pi)</math> may be a much smaller matrix so easier to compute with.

This is especially relevant to [[distance regular graph]]s, where the partition based on distance from a chosen vertex is equitable.  That makes for, besides simplified computation of eigenvalues, a simple diagram of the numerical properties of a [[distance regular graph]].<ref>Brouwer, Cohen, and Neumaier (1989).</ref>

* Chris Godsil and Gordon Royle (2001), ''Algebraic Graph Theory'',  Graduate Texts in Math., Vol. 207,  Springer-Verlag, New York.
* Brendan McKay (1981), Practical graph isomorphism, ''Congressus Numerantium'', Vol. 30 (1981), pp.&nbsp;45–87.
